UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION




Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address
                                                                   Docket No. ER26-3380-000
Resource Adequacy and Large Loads




Proposal Of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. to
Establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service
                                                                   Docket No. ER26-3515-000
and a Large Load Registry to Address System
Reliability




                          SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS OF VOLTUS

                              IN RESPONSE TO PJM’S ANSWERS

       Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s

(“FERC’s” or “Commission’s”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, Voltus, Inc., (“Voltus”) hereby

moves for leave to answer and respectfully submits these brief comments in response to PJM

Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM’s”) answers filed September 10, 2026, and September 23, 2026,

in the above-captioned Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”) and Interim Resource

Adequacy Service (“IRAS”) proceedings, respectively. Voltus’s purpose is to supplement the

record related to Demand Resource and DER Capacity Aggregation Resource (“DR/DER”)

eligibility criteria in light of PJM’s updates, in order to assist the Commission in ensuring

alignment between these two closely related frameworks and enable the urgent addition of new

capacity to the PJM system in furtherance of overall RBP/IRAS design objectives.



                                                                                           1
           I.​    PJM’S ANSWERS IN THE INTERLINKED RBP AND IRAS DOCKETS
                 HELPFULLY ADDRESS DR/DER ELIGIBILITY BUT INTRODUCE A
                 KEY DISCREPANCY
        At issue is the allowable composition of DR/DER resources that may be considered new

system capacity that, if bilaterally contracted by a relevant large load, may perform two distinct

but related functions: (1) reducing the RBP procurement target—the Qualified RBP Offset

(“QRBPO”) function—and (2) reducing the large load’s IRAS curtailment exposure (more

accurately, the volume of IRAS MW assigned to the Electric Distributor zone/area in which the

large load is located)—the Bring Your Own New Capacity (“BYONC”) function.

        PJM’s original proposed tariff revisions to implement RBP did not specify the allowable

composition of DR/DER resources for QRBPO purposes,1 and the original proposed IRAS tariff

revisions appeared to expressly limit the composition of DR/DER resources to retail customer

sites that had never before been registered toward a capacity resource.2 “Dormant” sites—those

that had once supported a wholesale capacity resource but had since terminated

participation—were disallowed, as were, it appeared, capacity increases at existing sites tied to

new assets. These exclusions represented a departure from positions PJM had taken during the

stakeholder process and amounted to undue discrimination between the treatment of DR/DER

and utility-scale generation/storage, since PJM had proposed to include the repowering of

deactivated generators and various forms of uprates/increments at utility-scale facilities as

allowable new capacity for BYONC, QRBPO, and even RBP offer purposes, and had not




1
  PJM RBP Filing of July 31, 2026, in Docket No. ER26-3380 (hereinafter “PJM RBP Filing”), proposed Tariff
Attachment DD, section 18.2(b)(vi) (specifying QRBPO resource eligibility); see also Comments of Voltus of Aug.
21, 2026, in Docket No. ER26-3380 (hereinafter “Voltus RBP Comments”) at § II.A, pp. 4-5.
2
  PJM IRAS Filing of Aug. 13, 2026, in Docket No. ER26-3515 (hereinafter “PJM IRAS Filing”), proposed Tariff
Attachment DD-4, section VI(b)(ii) (specifying BYONC resource eligibility for DR/DER); see also Comments of
Voltus of Sept. 3, 2026, in Docket No. ER26-3515 (hereinafter “Voltus IRAS Comments”) at § II.A, pp. 7-9.

                                                                                                             2
 justified why analogous behind-the-meter capabilities should be removed from the RBP/IRAS

framework.3

          Voltus sought clarification in both dockets. In the RBP docket, PJM’s answer introduced

language to explicitly identify increments in capacity tied to new generation or storage

investments behind-the-meter as eligible for the QRBPO function.4 The proposed update did not,

however, take up “reactivations” of dormant DR sites.5 PJM’s answer in the IRAS docket

addressed Voltus’s requested revisions on DR/DER BYONC eligibility in full, clarifying that

asset-backed increments at existing sites qualify, and explicitly “agree[ing]” with Voltus that

          “dormant” registered locations should be allowed to be reactivated to support
          BYONC resources. Such locations are not currently supporting Capacity
          Resources, and therefore any capacity capability they can provide would be new
          as compared to the capacity on the system for the 2026/2027 Delivery Year.6
          PJM suggests to reflect this capability in tariff language by allowing “locations that did

not support a Capacity Resource, a Peak Shaving Adjustment, or Price Responsive Demand for

the 2026/2027 Delivery Year . . .” to support BYONC arrangements.7

           Voltus thanks PJM for these clarifications and substantive modifications which take

several     steps   towards parity between          demand-side and utility-scale resources for

BYONC/QRBPO purposes. However, if the adjustments PJM has proposed in its separately filed

answers are taken up in the final tariff exactly as written, the reactivation of dormant DR/DER

locations will fulfill the BYONC but not the QRBPO function. This discrepancy contravenes

intended design, with material impact, as further discussed below.

                                                                                                    3
         II.​   VOLTUS SUGGESTS A STRAIGHTFORWARD EDIT TO ADDRESS THE
               IDENTIFIED DISCREPANCY
       Voltus respectfully but strongly recommends one additional, critical revision to PJM’s

proposed tariff language as revised by its RBP Answer, to align incentives and ensure a

continuity in PJM’s overall approach: PJM’s QRBPO resource eligibility definition should allow

for the reactivation of a “dormant” registered location, in line with the same allowance PJM has

supported on the BYONC side.

       The following straightforward edit to proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, section

18.2(b)(vi) would achieve the necessary alignment:

       (vi) Planned Demand Resource or Planned DER Capacity Aggregation Resources,
       as described in the RAA, Schedule 6 and Schedule 6.2, where such incremental
       capacity are not reliant on locations which previously provided capacity for the
       2026/2027 Delivery Year unless such previous location represents additional
       capacity resulting from an investment in new generation or new storage resources
       at that location.
The above redline takes as its starting point the updated language PJM proposed in its RBP

Answer and implements the same definition of a “dormant” location that PJM provided in its

IRAS Answer.


       III.​   ENABLING THE SAME RESOURCES TO SUPPORT BOTH QRBPO
               AND BYONC ALIGNS INCENTIVES AND SUPPORTS THE OVERALL
               DESIGN OF PJM’S LARGE LOAD RESOURCE ADEQUACY
               SOLUTIONS
       Without this or similar adjustment in the final tariff filing, BYONC arrangements

incorporating reactivated locations will not function to reduce the volume of RBP central

procurement, resulting in duplicative matching of new capacity volumes to DY27/28 and

DY28/29 load additions, along with the unnecessary imposition of socialized risk across all

ratepayers in the PJM footprint. It is the shared preference of a wide range of stakeholders to

shift capacity procurement from RBP to bilateral transactions so as to avoid this socialization and


                                                                                                 4
 make good on the Ratepayer Protection Pledge by ensuring that large loads bear the costs

associated with serving their growth. To effectuate this shift from centralized to private-market

funding, the same bilateral contracts that relieve a load of IRAS exposure and return the load and

its matched supply to RPM must also decrement the RBP target. This requires that the

underlying BYONC and QRBPO resource eligibility criteria be the same. Indeed, for

utility-scale generation and storage, PJM has defined eligibility with exactly the same tariff

language for both functions.8 Thus each and every generation/storage MW that can support

BYONC is also eligible as a QRBPO MW—provided, of course, that commercial operation date

(“COD”) meets the QRBPO requirement. This same alignment is necessary on the DR/DER

side, and it is Voltus’s understanding from stakeholder conversations with PJM staff that

alignment of BYONC and QRBPO resource eligibility has been PJM’s ongoing design intention.


        IV.​    A FAILURE TO RESOLVE THE IDENTIFIED DISCREPANCY WILL
                DISINCENTIVIZE LARGE VOLUMES OF POTENTIAL NEW
                CAPACITY WITH NEAR-TERM AVAILABILITY, FRUSTRATING
                RELIABILITY AND AFFORDABILITY GOALS
        Note also that the specific category here under consideration—the capabilities of dormant

locations—is uniquely relevant in the context of QRBPO. As Voltus has explained elsewhere,

DR/DER aggregations are functionally precluded from direct RBP participation.9 Yet they

represent the set of resources with perhaps the earliest average commercial operation date

(because DR/DER aggregations take advantage of capabilities already “latent” on the grid) and

thus are among the most attractive resources for large load growth that will be subject to IRAS in

the 27/28 and 28/29 Delivery Years. These near-term loads are subject to uncertain, 15-year cost

allocation from RBP in addition to IRAS curtailment, and are looking for resources that limit

8
  Compare proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.2(b)(i)-(v) in PJM’s RBP Filing with proposed Tariff,
Attachment DD-4, section VI(b)(i)(1)-(5).
9
  See Voltus RBP Comments at § III.A, pp. 10-13.

                                                                                                        5
 both exposures. Allowing dormant locations to qualify as QRBPO is therefore crucial to

effectively incentivizing large loads and aggregators to reactivate this capacity. Note that without

such allowance, a large load prioritizing RBP cost avoidance will prefer a new capacity resource

with a June 1, 2032, COD over DR/DER reactivation capacity available in 2027/2028—a

perverse outcome for grid reliability and ratepayer affordability.

          The volumes at issue are not small. Voltus estimates that dormant commercial and

industrial locations are capable of providing in the range of 2 GW of new capacity given

BYONC price signals.10 Incentivizing such capacity to be brought online in the next two delivery

years will relieve grid strain immediately and improve near-term affordability.

         Indeed, new capacity contracted to come online in the 27/28 and 28/29 Delivery Years

has a unique ratepayer affordability benefit. Beginning with Delivery Year 29/30, New Large

Loads will be excluded from the Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) by default and brought back

to the Variable Resource Requirement (“VRR”) curve only if matched by new capacity that

enters the relevant auction as a price taker. The expected impact will be price neutral. But since

New Large Loads have not been excluded from 27/28 and 28/29 RPM, any new capacity

contracted in time to enter, as price taker, the 27/28 and 28/29 Incremental Auctions will exert

downward pressure on the capacity costs borne by all ratepayers as 27/28 and 28/29 RPM cost

allocation, with the potential to provide immediate relief.

         Counting demand-side reactivations as QRBPO will have the additional impact of

protecting “native” load from the risk of RBP cost-shifting over the next 15 years. For all these

reasons, affording DR/DER reactivations equivalent BYONC and QRBPO treatment is not a

drafting detail but an impactful policy choice.

10
   This estimate is based on an analysis of Voltus’s past customers and their reasons for dropping out of DR capacity,
Voltus’s share of the DR capacity market in PJM, and external data points. See also Voltus IRAS Comments at p. 11
(referencing statistics on past DR participation volumes).

                                                                                                                    6
          V.​   CONCLUSION
       PJM has proposed to allow reactivated DR/DER locations for BYONC but not QRBPO

purposes, introducing a discrepancy that impedes the overall design of the RBP/IRAS

framework. The impact is highly material, because reactivations are among the only resources

available to match 27/28 and 28/29 large load additions, and they are available to do so in

significant volumes. However, because DR/DER resources are functionally excluded from RBP,

DR/DER reactivations are only able to match large load additions and reduce IRAS exposure via

bilateral contracts. Unless these same bilaterals also reduce RBP cost exposure, large loads will

be disincentivized from procuring DR/DER reactivations as compared to other resources. The

final result will be less new capacity coming online over the next several delivery years and a

reduction in the volume of emergency DR available for PJM to dispatch. The negative impacts

on reliability, near-term affordability via RPM price impacts, and long-term RBP cost-shifting

risk may be avoided by the simple tariff revision Voltus has recommended herein. Voltus

respectfully asks that PJM take up such revision, or similar, with Commission support.

       Voltus deeply appreciates PJM’s ongoing collaboration with stakeholders on effective

RBP/IRAS design and thanks the Commission for this opportunity to supplement the record.



                                                           Respectfully submitted,
